His friend came back; they made a list of people Bill had hurt, and Bill became willing to go to them and admit his wrongs (p. 13). 8da4c99f6dd4: What is the "spiritual awakening" in Step 12?
9a751a3f6953: Step Twelve says the awakening comes "as the result of these steps" (p. 60). It follows the work of the first eleven Steps; it isn't a precondition for starting them.
0dd26fa6d918: The Big Book's Appendix II, "Spiritual Experience," says the book uses "spiritual experience" and "spiritual awakening" for the same thing: "the personality change sufficient to bring about recovery from alcoholism" (p. 567).
3e205fca5c28: Most such changes are slow, what William James called the "educational variety" (p. 567). Friends often notice before the person does (p. 567).
38dff0090ac8: Members usually find an inner resource they hadn't suspected, which they come to identify with their own idea of a Power greater than themselves (pp. 567–568).
38a8e440cfc0: The appendix was added after the first printing of 1939, because that printing had given readers the wrong idea (p. 567). Its main points, in order:
460e26db3394: The terms "spiritual experience" and "spiritual awakening" are used throughout the book, and a careful reading shows the personality change behind recovery "has manifested itself among us in many different forms" (p. 567).
9b7423b13011: The first printing left many readers thinking these changes had to be "sudden and spectacular upheavals" (p. 567). "Happily for everyone, this conclusion is erroneous" (p. 567).
37162c5b99b1: Sudden transformations, "though frequent, are by no means the rule" (p. 567). Most are of the "educational variety because they develop slowly over a period of time" (p. 567).
038a01171d49: The person finally realizes he has "undergone a profound alteration in his reaction to life" that he couldn't have brought about alone (p. 567).
53fb2f22a52a: Members find they have "tapped an unsuspected … inner resource which they presently identify with their own conception of a Power greater than themselves" (pp. 567–568). "Our more religious members call it God-consciousness" (p. 568).
86d40129e0d8: Anyone who honestly faces his problems in the light of A.A. experience can recover, "provided he does not close his mind to all spiritual concepts" (p. 568). "Willingness, honesty and open mindedness are the essentials of recovery" (p. 568).

90e2406ecd1e: What does "the spiritual life is not a theory. We have to live it" refer to?
eb84ce468820: The lines are on page 83 of the Big Book, in Chapter 6, "Into Action," in the part about making amends at home to the wife and family (pp. 82–83).
528032808042: Just before them, the book tells the recovering man to sit down with his family, look honestly at the past without criticizing them, and ask each morning to be shown "the way of patience, tolerance, kindliness and love" (p. 83).
53994ddfa9cf: Just after, it says not to push spiritual principles on the family or talk to them constantly about spiritual matters: "Our behavior will convince them more than our words." (p. 83)
abbeb719529e: So the context confirms the usual reading, that the spiritual life is something you do and not only something you believe, and makes it specific. In its place, "live it" means at home, through how you treat your family, instead of preaching to them.
4cea1b4473d5: The amends section of Chapter 6 deals with creditors, enemies, legal trouble and infidelity, and then turns to the home: "If we have no such complication, there is plenty we should do at home." (p. 82)
6e81edba769b: The book answers the man who thinks staying sober is enough. He must stay sober, "for there will be no home if he doesn't" (p. 82), but he's still a long way from making good to the people he treated so badly. "The alcoholic is like a tornado roaring his way through the lives of others." (p. 82) A man who says sobriety is enough is like the farmer who comes up from his storm cellar, finds his home in ruins, and remarks to his wife that it's grand the wind has stopped (p. 82).
c748c1d22d3d: Then page 83, in order: 1. <0>Reconstruction.</0> "Yes, there is a long period of reconstruction ahead." (p. 83) "We must take the lead." (p. 83) A remorseful mumble that we're sorry "won't fill the bill at all" (p. 83). 2. <1>The family talk.</1> Sit down with the family and frankly look at the past as we now see it, "being very careful not to criticize them" (p. 83). Their defects may be glaring, but our actions are likely partly responsible (p. 83). 3. <2>The morning prayer.</2> "So we clean house with the family," asking each morning in meditation for patience, tolerance, kindliness and love (p. 83). 4. <3>The line.</3> "The spiritual life is not a theory. We have to live it." (p. 83) 5. <4>Don't preach.</4> Unless the family wants to live on spiritual principles, "we think we ought not to urge them" (p. 83). Don't talk incessantly to them about spiritual matters. "They will change in time." (p. 83) Behaviour convinces more than words, and "ten or twenty years of drunkenness would make a skeptic out of anyone" (p. 83).
9e476f05bc4a: The paragraph after that covers wrongs that can never be fully righted (p. 83), and then come the Promises (pp. 83–84).
b00ae10c8443: Chapter 9, "The Family Afterward," gives the other side of it. A father who has a sudden spiritual experience may become a religious enthusiast who talks about spiritual matters "morning, noon and night" (p. 128) and tells his family to find God in a hurry. The book's answer is that "a spiritual life which does not include his family obligations may not be so perfect after all" (p. 129). The writers say they believe God would like them to keep their heads in the clouds with Him, "but that our feet ought to be firmly planted on earth" (p. 130). "We have found nothing incompatible between a powerful spiritual experience and a life of sane and happy usefulness." (p. 130)
f884d5e4f1c7: Chapter 9 is gentle with this father, though, and its advice here is mostly to the family. If they cooperate he will soon see that his spiritual growth is lopsided (p. 129). Meanwhile they "should let him have his head" (p. 129), and the book judges him on a firmer foundation than the man who puts business or professional success "ahead of spiritual development" (p. 130).
9117d8e0e7c0: It confirms it and narrows it. Quoted alone, the line works as a general saying about practice over belief, and the book would agree with that. In its place it has a particular target: the man who thinks sobriety is enough at home, or who talks about his new spiritual life instead of changing how he treats his family. Living it, there, means patience and kindness at home, and leaving the family free.

cb7b939af871: The phrase is used once in the 1939 program text (pp. 1–164), on page 64, at the start of the Fourth Step inventory: "When the spiritual malady is overcome, we straighten out mentally and physically." (p. 64)
0f5041213d81: In place, it's tied to resentment. The sentence before says of resentment, "From it stem all forms of spiritual disease" (p. 64).
e91fa4e078ca: The passage adds the spiritual to the mental and physical; it doesn't replace them: "we have been not only mentally and physically ill, we have been spiritually sick" (p. 64).
cf02bd8f694d: The book doesn't define the phrase further. The pages around it describe the sickness as self-centredness showing up as resentment and fear (pp. 62–68), and the remedy as the inventory and the Steps that follow.
e15c0cbaaf33: The book has just said that self was what defeated us, and turns to its "common manifestations" (p. 64). Then, in four sentences:
9e70f479edbc: "It destroys more alcoholics than anything else." (p. 64)
8f9426388e2b: "From it stem all forms of spiritual disease, for we have been not only mentally and physically ill, we have been spiritually sick." (p. 64)
37253e799ff1: "When the spiritual malady is overcome, we straighten out mentally and physically." (p. 64)
9012d1affaf9: So "the spiritual malady" in sentence 4 points back to the "spiritual disease" and being "spiritually sick" of sentence 3, which the book says stems from resentment.
c14a599e48e2: What the sickness looks like in the pages around it
117a49af1ed4: <0>Its root is self.</0> Two pages earlier: "Selfishness—self-centeredness! That, we think, is the root of our troubles." (p. 62)
10069b6dcae8: <0>It cuts a person off.</0> Harbouring resentment, "we shut ourselves off from the sunlight of the Spirit" (p. 66), and "The insanity of alcohol returns and we drink again." (p. 66)
91d6953dec34: <0>Fear runs through it.</0> "This short word somehow touches about every aspect of our lives." (p. 67)
5b36287b96a6: <0>It isn't only alcoholics who have it.</0> The book asks the reader to see that the people who wronged us "were perhaps spiritually sick" (p. 66), and "they, like ourselves, were sick too" (p. 67).
d27dc2fcb4af: Everywhere else in the main text, "malady" means alcoholism itself. Chapter 2 says that once "this malady has a real hold," drinkers are baffled (p. 23). Chapter 7 tells the helper to speak of alcoholism "as an illness, a fatal malady" (p. 92). Chapter 10 talks about explaining "alcoholism, the malady" to an employer (p. 138). The Foreword to the Second Edition (1955) says Dr. Bob began "to pursue the spiritual remedy for his malady" (p. xvi). Page 64 is the one place in the program text where the word is qualified as "spiritual." (One fourth-edition personal story, "A Vision of Recovery," uses the phrase too: the member writes that "the spiritual malady should be my main concern" (p. 499). That's a member's account from the stories, which change by edition, not the 1939 text.)
c61c4baaf5ed: The book doesn't use those words. What it says about alcoholism as a whole, to a reader who finds he can't quit or can't control the amount, is that "you may be suffering from an illness which only a spiritual experience will conquer" (p. 44), and that it is an illness of body and mind (p. xxvi). On p. 64 it says that underneath the mental and physical illness there was a spiritual one, and that dealing with that one straightens out the others.
ef741b080968: The book is careful not to make that a cure. It makes room for medical help: although the members work out their solution "on the spiritual as well as an altruistic plane" (p. xxvi), they "favor hospitalization for the alcoholic who is very jittery or befogged" (p. xxvi). And after the Steps, "We are not cured of alcoholism." (p. 85)
f058190d9b88: The book doesn't give a separate method for the spiritual malady. The sentence sits at the start of the inventory, and what follows is the inventory itself: listing resentments, seeing the people involved as sick, praying, finding our own part, and looking at fear and sex conduct (pp. 64–70). After that come the Fifth through Ninth Steps in Chapter 6. See <0>How does the Big Book say to do Step 4?</0>
097a785e5352: It confirms that the book puts a spiritual sickness beneath the drinking. It complicates the shorthand "alcoholism is a spiritual malady." In the program text, the phrase is used once. It's tied to resentment and self, and it's named <0>alongside</0> being mentally and physically ill, not instead of them.

1d62674fcf6a: Where the word is, and isn't
fd1a6bb09261: Searching the whole fourth edition, every use of "sponsor" or "sponsorship" is in the personal stories (from page 165 on). There are none in the 164 pages that set out the program, none in the forewords, and none in the seven appendices.
7443289625e3: The program's own instructions for helping another alcoholic are in Chapter 7, "Working With Others" (pp. 89–103). That chapter never uses the word. It describes reaching a man who is still drinking, who owes you nothing (p. 94), and who is free to go to someone else when he's ready to tell his story (p. 96). See: <0>What does Step 12 really say?</0>
d916be8dbcc4: "The Vicious Cycle" (Part I, "Pioneers of A.A.") is the story of a man who got sober on January 8, 1938, more than a year before the fellowship had the name Alcoholics Anonymous (p. 220).
d3c0d1f97263: His sponsor was Jackie, the man who came to him while he was still drinking. Jackie "brought in many of our original members, yet he himself could not make it and died of alcoholism" (p. 220). Jackie had been sober only a month or so when he carried the message (p. 226). Two weeks later Jackie got drunk, and the writer says he had "become the sponsor of my sponsor" (p. 226).
6334dfedb29e: In that story a sponsor isn't an experienced member who manages a newcomer's program. He's whoever went out and brought the message to a drunk, even someone barely sober himself. That is Chapter 7's work.
331a4d441feb: "He Sold Himself Short" (also in Part I) describes Akron in 1937, before the Big Book was written (p. 260). Before the writer was allowed to his first meeting, eight or nine members came to see him, one after another (p. 262). Then Dr. Bob spent an afternoon taking him through the program as it was then, six steps, the last being "Continued work with other alcoholics" (p. 263). The writer calls that afternoon "this type of sponsorship" (p. 263), and adds that Dr. Bob "always emphasized the religious angle very strongly" (p. 263). Here the sponsor is the most experienced member there was, leading a newcomer through every step, but it is one afternoon, after which the man went home to Chicago to start a group (pp. 263–264).
260851774116: Sponsorship as many rooms describe it today, a standing relationship with a senior member who guides you through the Steps over months, isn't described in the Big Book's program at all. Where the word appears in the earliest stories, it describes someone going out to a drinker and carrying the message, which is what Chapter 7 tells every member to do, and, in Akron, an older member taking a newcomer through the program in a single sitting. Neither is the months-long arrangement.

eb6b8a308797: My husband (or wife) drinks. What does the Big Book say to do?
2c86c2bb2568: Chapter 8, "To Wives" (pp. 104–121), is the Big Book's answer. It was written in 1939 in the voice of members' wives, addressed to the wives of men who drink (the later history books say Bill W. wrote it), and its suggestions "may be adapted" for anyone living with an alcoholic, man or woman (p. 104, later-edition note).
8b6f8f9a1b05: Its core advice: don't be angry, don't nag or tell him what he must do about his drinking, don't let his drinking ruin your life with your children and friends, and treat him as a sick person, "as though he had pneumonia" (p. 108).
c7caf4abd820: It also makes an exception for a husband who is "thoroughly bad-intentioned" (p. 108), on whom no amount of patience will make any difference: "If you are positive he is one of this type you may feel you had better leave." (p. 108).
3c39cb58e07c: It ends by urging the wife to try the program herself: the wives found that putting spiritual principles to work "solves our problems too" (p. 116). Al-Anon, which uses the general principles of the A.A. program as a guide, was formed about thirteen years after the chapter was written and is entirely separate from A.A. (p. 121, later-edition note).
e9fa7e64c332: Who wrote it, and for whom
a6812bdd5e7c: The chapter is in the voice of "wives of Alcoholics Anonymous" (p. 104), some of whose problems had been solved and some not. The book itself doesn't say who held the pen. Both later history books say Bill W. wrote it: "Bill himself wrote the chapter that came to be called 'To Wives'" (<0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0>, 1980), and Lois W. recalled, "Bill wrote it, and I was mad" (<1>Pass It On</1>, 1984); she had offered to write it, and he wanted it in the same style as the rest of the book (<2>Pass It On</2>). What they say, they write, "will apply to nearly everyone bound by ties of blood or affection to an alcoholic" (p. 104). A later-edition footnote says it was written when there were few women in A.A. and so assumes the drinker is the husband, but "many of the suggestions given here may be adapted to help the person who lives with a woman alcoholic" (p. 104).
aa64bc9fd2e3: The opening pages are a frank list of what the wives lived with and how they reacted: lies to protect pride and reputation, begging, patience, striking out, running away, retaliatory affairs, loneliness, money that "melted like snow in June" (p. 106), violence toward the children and the home, and at the end "commitment to health resorts, sanitariums, hospitals, and jails" (p. 107). Many of their mistakes, they say, "rose out of ignorance of alcoholism" (p. 107).
1d4084c3299f: <0>He is sick.</0> "Try not to condemn your alcoholic husband no matter what he says or does." (p. 108). "He is just another very sick, unreasonable person." (p. 108). "Treat him, when you can, as though he had pneumonia." (p. 108).
7d5210a183ff: <0>Except when he means harm.</0> "We realize some men are thoroughly bad-intentioned, that no amount of patience will make any difference." (p. 108). Such a man may use the chapter "as a club over your head" (p. 108), and the wife shouldn't let him. "Is it right to let him ruin your life and the lives of your children?" (p. 108).
ad46297de526: <0>Know what you're dealing with.</0> The chapter describes four kinds of drinking husband: the heavy drinker who may moderate or stop; the one showing loss of control, with "the earmarks of a real alcoholic" (p. 109); the one much further gone, of whom "You can be quite hopeful" (p. 110); and the one whose family has despaired, who may still recover (p. 110).
d350f30fdd36: <0>Never angry.</0> "The first principle of success is that you should never be angry." (p. 111). Even if she has to leave temporarily, she should go without rancor (p. 111).
11637eae09e3: <0>Don't tell him what to do.</0> "Our next thought is that you should never tell him what he must do about his drinking." (p. 111). If he sees her as a nag, her chances of helping "may be zero" (p. 111).
99e304489add: <0>Your own life.</0> "Be determined that your husband's drinking is not going to spoil your relations with your children or your friends." (p. 111). "It is possible to have a full and useful life, though your husband continues to drink." (p. 111). "Do not set your heart on reforming your husband." (p. 111).
27a4f65121d0: <0>When he's ready to talk.</0> Let him bring it up. Suggest he read the book, or just the chapter on alcoholism (pp. 111–112). For the second kind of husband, after a binge, ask whether he would really like to stop for good, not for her sake (p. 112). If he isn't interested, leave him alone; "the more you hurry him the longer his recovery may be delayed" (p. 113).
48b8d41e5e11: <0>Don't lie for him.</0> Avoid covering for him with his employer and friends; "Whenever possible, let your husband explain." (p. 115). Quietly letting friends know the nature of his illness ends much of the embarrassment (p. 115).
2658e736fe22: <0>Children.</0> Unless they need protection from their father, don't take sides in his arguments with them while he's drinking (p. 115).

9f4fec1af6ab: Read straight through, the fifteen pages work as a field guide:
e8cfaebdb53b: <0>Find drinkers who want to stop.</0> Ask doctors, ministers and hospitals (p. 89). Don't try to persuade someone who doesn't want to quit (p. 90).
605c8123dcd8: <0>Learn about the man first, and choose your moment.</0> Talk with the person closest to him, wait for the end of a binge, and never force yourself on him (p. 90). An approach through a doctor or an institution is better than through his family (p. 91).
9d9664b0475e: <0>Talk about your own drinking, not his.</0> See him alone. Tell him enough of your story that he'll start telling his, and for now say nothing about how you got sober (p. 91).
b04578d37e53: <0>Let him decide whether he's an alcoholic.</0> Describe the illness from your own experience, and don't label him (p. 92).
fb9159ca9754: <0>Tell him how you recovered only when he asks</0> (p. 93). Outline the program of action and say why you're helping (p. 94).
e7d46eb4bb2e: <0>Leave him free.</0> Make it plain he's under no obligation and needn't see you again (p. 94). Don't wear out your welcome or rush him (p. 95).
1b1e8a7da334: <0>If he isn't interested, find someone who is.</0> The book is blunt about it: spending too long on one person "is to deny some other alcoholic an opportunity to live and be happy" (p. 96).
aa70fb7144c7: <0>Be ready for what it costs.</0> Lost sleep, your money and your home, trips to courts, hospitals and jails (p. 97). Help his family even if he keeps drinking (p. 97).
0133a3e4f5bc: <0>Go wherever you can be useful.</0> Even "the most sordid spot on earth," if you're there to help (p. 102).
a0d6275d821c: <0>It isn't sponsorship.</0> The word doesn't appear in the chapter. The relationship it describes is with a man who may not be in A.A. at all yet, who owes you nothing (p. 94), and who is free to go to someone else when he's ready to make his decision and tell his story (p. 96). Nothing in these pages describes an ongoing arrangement with a member already in the rooms.
80cc3f11dd5d: <0>It isn't a private spiritual experience.</0> The Step opens with a spiritual awakening, and the Big Book's own appendix on that phrase, written after the first printing (p. 567), says most such changes are of the "educational variety" and develop slowly over time, not as sudden upheavals (p. 567). The action the Step asks for is carrying the message.
79be20c9a1d9: <0>It isn't self-serving.</0> The chapter's first line says that working with other alcoholics protects the helper's own sobriety (p. 89), and it says so again: your effort "plays a vital part in your own recovery" (p. 94), and "Helping others is the foundation stone of your recovery" (p. 97). Taken alone, those lines can sound like "help others to keep yourself sober." But the chapter doesn't stop there. It asks the newcomer to "place the welfare of other people ahead of his own" (p. 94), it lists what the helper gives up (p. 97), and it says "Do not think of what you will get out of the occasion. Think of what you can bring to it" (p. 102). The helper's sobriety is real and named, but the chapter's stated aim is the other man: "To be helpful is our only aim" (p. 89).
25c25fd8b32c: God is mentioned, and the helper is told to "stress the spiritual feature freely" when describing his own recovery (p. 93). The chapter is also plain that recovery rests on God: the helper is to "Burn the idea into the consciousness of every man that he can get well regardless of anyone," and "The only condition is that he trust in God and clean house" (p. 98); his recovery "is dependent upon his relationship with God" (p. 100). Use everyday language, and don't raise theological issues "no matter what your own convictions are" (p. 93). You're not there to instruct him in religion (p. 93). "We have no monopoly on God" (p. 95). "Never talk down to an alcoholic from any moral or spiritual hilltop" (p. 95). The chapter forbids preaching. What it asks for is rescue.

678f6a59d1f4: The Big Book calls the Steps suggestions. It introduces them as "the steps we took, which are suggested as a program of recovery" (p. 59), and says on its last page that the whole book is meant only to suggest (p. 164).

1efb846ae4d6: But "suggested" doesn't mean "optional and harmless to skip." The same pages report, from the writers' experience, that half measures got them nowhere and that newcomers who skipped the Fifth Step nearly always got drunk. The Steps are offered as what worked, not as rules anyone enforces.
2fc183720962: The wording around the Steps is consistently the language of suggestion and experience: - The list is introduced as the steps "we took," suggested "as a program of recovery" (p. 59). - Right after the list, the book answers the reader who thinks it's too much: no one has kept "anything like perfect adherence to these principles" (p. 60). They are "guides to progress," and the aim is "spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection" (p. 60). - Step Twelve is introduced as "our twelfth suggestion" (p. 89). Steps Ten and Eleven are each said to "suggest" (pp. 84–85). - On a hard question about amends at home, the writers say they "wish to lay down no rule of any sort" (p. 81). - The book's closing page says the whole book is meant only as a suggestion, and that the writers know only a little; more will be disclosed to the reader and to them (p. 164). - To employers: when the man is given the book, no one should tell him he must follow it. "The man must decide for himself" (p. 144).
992d07e2e14d: What the book says about skipping them
0f12da4da367: The same text is just as plain that leaving Steps out has a cost. It reports what happened to its members; it doesn't threaten anyone. - The chapter opens by saying the writers have rarely "seen a person fail who has thoroughly followed our path" (p. 58). The writers ask the reader to be "fearless and thorough from the very start" (p. 58), and say "Half measures availed us nothing" (p. 59). - Some members looked for "an easier, softer way. But we could not" (p. 58). - On the Fifth Step: "If we skip this vital step, we may not overcome drinking" (p. 72). Newcomers who tried to keep certain facts about their lives to themselves nearly always got drunk (pp. 72–73). - On self-centredness: "We must, or it kills us!" (p. 62). - Appendix II, written after the first printing (p. 567), says willingness, honesty and open-mindedness "are the essentials of recovery. But these are indispensable" (p. 568).
a4d5fdc11777: The text doesn't make the Steps into rules. No one in A.A. is given the power to enforce them, and the book insists the reader decides for himself (p. 144). It also doesn't treat them as optional extras. It offers them as a record of what a group of alcoholics did and what happened to those who did and didn't, and leaves the choice with the reader. Where the book uses "must," it's describing the alcoholic's situation as the writers found it, not giving an order from an authority.

dd0ee4229a16: <0>1. The "Thirteenth Way Out" (1946).</0> In his Grapevine article "Anonymity" (1946), Bill tells how the book got its title. A narrow vote had favored "The Way Out," but the Library of Congress already had twelve books by that name: "we shivered at the possibility of being the 'Thirteenth Way Out'" (P-17, "Anonymity," 1946). So the book, and the fellowship, became "Alcoholics Anonymous." Bill tells the same story in <1>A.A. Comes of Age</1> (1957). This isn't a step at all. It's a joke about a book title.
3e10fb9bacda: <0>2. Clubs as a "Thirteenth Step" (1947).</0> In "Clubs in A.A." (1947), Bill writes that so many members value clubs that "we might conceive them as a central A.A. institution — a sort of 'Thirteenth Step' of our recovery program without which the other Twelve Steps wouldn't work" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.," 1947). He raises it as the far end of the pro-club view: some enthusiasts act as if club life alone could handle the drinking problem, and they "are apt to depend upon clubs rather than upon the A.A. program" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.," 1947). He then gives the opposite view and settles on a middle ground. Members who want clubs should have them, but clubs should be separately incorporated and kept apart from the groups' A.A. affairs, "to separate the material from the spiritual" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.," 1947). (See <1>What did Bill W. say about clubs and A.A.?</1>)
b7615c7ae3af: <0>3. "Victor" and "Lil" (written 1980, about 1935).</0> <1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1> tells of a former Akron mayor and "the first woman to seek help," two of the alcoholics around Akron in the summer and fall of 1935 "who didn't jell" (<2>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</2>, 1980). "Together, Victor and the lady known as Lil started out to write the 'thirteenth step,' long before the first twelve were ever thought of" (<3>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</3>, 1980). The book adds that "they say it began in Dr. Bob's office—on his examination table" (<4>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</4>, 1980). The night ended with Lil, drunk, grabbing pills and lunging for a window. Bill later recalled that they were all "scandalized by the episode" (<5>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</5>, 1980), and "they say" Dr. Bob was wary of alcoholic women for a long time afterward, though he still tried to help any who came along. The book passes the story on as A.A. "folklore" and as hearsay ("they say"). It doesn't define the phrase. It uses it knowingly, for a man and a woman pairing off, and expects the reader to get the joke.

d8cc26aaf7a9: Can anyone be thrown out of A.A.?
3ea61b581b3f: No one can be expelled from A.A. itself. The Long Form of Tradition Three says "we may refuse none who wish to recover" (p. 563), and that membership should never depend on money or conformity.
d7e67205552e: Bill W., writing in 1946: a member "is a member as long as he says he is" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946).
b75965ab84f8: That isn't the same as putting up with anything at a meeting. In 1946 a member who kept turning up drunk could be "led outside" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946), then welcomed back the next day if sober. A club, which is separate from A.A., could bar him. Neither takes away his membership in A.A.
a700a56da090: Bill was honest that in 1946 this view was "not yet unanimous" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946) and membership rules still existed in places. The Tradition is the lesson A.A. drew from those rules.
d3c9be50a172: Tradition Three in its original form says A.A.'s membership "ought to include all who suffer from alcoholism" (p. 563). From that it follows, in the Tradition's own word "Hence," that "we may refuse none who wish to recover" (p. 563). And membership should never "depend upon money or conformity" (p. 563): not on dues, and not on agreeing with anyone or behaving a certain way.
3ee413331139: The short form puts it as one requirement, "a desire to stop drinking" (p. 562). The Long Form puts it the other way round: there's no one A.A. may turn away.
dc28b45dd57e: Bill's Grapevine piece "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?" (1946) is the essay Tradition Three grew out of, and it's mostly about throwing people out.
c933a0cbc8a3: A few years earlier, the New York office had asked groups to send in their membership rules. Put together, the rules filled "a great many sheets of paper" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). If all of them had been in force at once, almost no alcoholic could have joined, and about nine-tenths of the oldest and best members "could never have got by!" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). Early members would have been put out for slipping too often, for bad morals, for mental troubles, or for not coming from the "better classes."
a0b46481177c: Bill describes groups going on "rule-making benders" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946): committees given power to filter out undesirables, elders casting out the troublemakers. It didn't work. The fights over enforcement turned out to be worse for the group "than the very worst that the worst ever did" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). Some of the people once judged hopeless became the group's most respected and best-loved members, and Bill calls those who condemned them "the Pharisees" whose false righteousness did the group "the deeper spiritual damage" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946).
266497b68740: His conclusion: "Our A.A. door stands wide open" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). A newcomer "signs nothing, agrees to nothing, promises nothing" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). He joins on his own say-so.
50ad295a17d2: A meeting, a club, and A.A.
67266884e932: The same essay draws the line that answers most real cases. A member who "persists in coming to meetings drunk" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946) may be led outside, but in most groups he can come back the next day if he's sober. "Though he may be thrown out of a club, nobody thinks of throwing him out of A.A." (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946).
fc27c5afb590: So three different things: - <0>A.A. membership</0> belongs to the person. No group, committee or office can take it away. - <1>A meeting</1> can ask someone who is disrupting it to leave for now. Bill's 1946 essay on money mentions a steward who can "eject a troublesome drunk" (P-17, "Money", 1946). How a group runs its own meetings is its own affair under Tradition Four (p. 563). - <2>A club</2> is a separate thing that the Long Form says should be "set apart" from A.A. (p. 564). It can have its own rules for its own premises.
b651800ffe34: Bill didn't pretend everyone agreed. The open door wasn't yet the universal practice, he wrote: "Membership rules still exist." (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946). He called the broad view "the main current of A.A. thought today" (P-17, "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946), while adding it was not yet unanimous.
4e1ae1f70ed4: The 1946–47 texts deal with drunkenness, slips, panhandling, gossip and "mental twists." They don't take up a member who puts other people in danger. They say a group can lead someone out of a meeting and that a group runs its own affairs, but they don't spell out more than that, and we won't add to them.
7567851d126a: In 1957 Bill summed up Tradition Three as: "You are an A.A. member if you say so" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957). 30009c3e390f: What does the Big Book say to employers?
f6ce42f4f5a1: Chapter 10, "To Employers" (pp. 136–150), is written by a member who had hired and fired hundreds of men before becoming an alcoholic himself. Its summary: "No man should be fired just because he is alcoholic." (p. 148). If he wants to stop, he should be given a real chance. If he can't or won't stop, "he should be discharged" (p. 148).
7c81159b9e76: It asks the employer to see alcoholism as an illness, not weakness or stubbornness, and to give a sick employee who wants to recover the same consideration as other ailing employees (pp. 139–141).
d7a683abfa32: Its suggested approach: be firm that the drinking must stop, don't lecture, make sure he really wants to quit, arrange medical treatment through a doctor, keep it confidential, and give him the book, without telling him he must follow it (pp. 141–145).
27c3450809b7: It warns against the opposite mistake too: covering for a man who doesn't want to stop. "You are not doing him a favor by keeping him on." (p. 141).
494f10a2dc3b: The chapter is one member's account; the book doesn't name him. <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) says only that "there is some reason to believe" Hank may have written it (<1>Pass It On</1>, 1984). As an assistant manager in a large corporation, he lost three exceptional men to alcoholism, each of whom took his own life after being let go, "because I did not understand alcoholism as I do now" (p. 137). Then he became an alcoholic himself. He tells of trying to help a banker friend understand a fellow executive's drinking: the bank was sure the man was done, because he had taken a cure and been told it was his last chance. The man drank again and was fired; afterward the members reached him (pp. 138–139).
c0d5f05a51e5: <0>Set your own drinking aside.</0> A moderate drinker can be more annoyed with an alcoholic than a teetotaler, because he controls his own drinking and "cannot see why it should be to anyone else, save the spineless and stupid" (p. 139).
59c4bf51be97: <0>Is he worth salvaging?</0> The alcoholic employee is often brilliant and quick, "imaginative and likeable" (p. 139). If he would be worth keeping without the drinking, should he have "the same consideration as other ailing employees?" (p. 140). If the reader isn't sure the man is sick and not just weak, the chapter suggests re-reading Chapters 2 and 3 (p. 140).
40dce601071a: <0>His past scrapes.</0> These can generally be charged "to the abnormal action of alcohol on his mind" (p. 140). Not all alcoholics are honest when sober, and some will take advantage of kindness. "If you are sure your man does not want to stop, he may as well be discharged, the sooner the better." (p. 141). The writer says being fired first, then shown the solution, might have brought him back "a well man" six months later (p. 141).
79d3a4647bf0: <0>Be firm.</0> Tell him you know about his drinking "and that it must stop" (p. 141); you'd like to keep him, but can't if he keeps drinking. "A firm attitude at this point has helped many of us." (p. 142).
90e2eeeff9d6: <0>Don't lecture.</0> Assure him you won't moralize or condemn, and explain alcoholism as an illness (p. 142).
bb965f02224e: <0>Probe whether he really wants to stop.</0> "Will he take every necessary step, submit to anything to get well, to stop drinking forever?" (p. 142). If he still thinks he can drink again, even beer, he may as well be discharged after his next bender (p. 142).
ab0abdb90c39: <0>Medical treatment, through a doctor.</0> For a man drinking or just off a spree, "a certain amount of physical treatment is desirable, even imperative" (p. 143), referred to the employer's own doctor. The employer may advance the cost, to be deducted later from his pay, so he feels responsible (p. 143). But "physical treatment is but a small part of the picture" (p. 143); he must undergo "a change of heart" (p. 143).
38c5e7a90a9e: <0>Keep it confidential.</0> Treat it as "a strictly personal matter" (p. 143), never discussed without his consent.
81c13e30c62f: <0>The book, not a command.</0> Give the book to his doctor and to him; "it is best that no one tell him he must abide by its suggestions" (p. 144). "The man must decide for himself." (p. 144). The writer doesn't offer the approach "as the last word on this subject" (p. 144): "After all, are you not looking for results rather than methods?" (p. 144).
f5ed2a20a612: <0>When he comes back.</0> Be ready to hear shocking things, such as a padded expense account; his new honesty demands it (p. 145).
e91c993b647f: Protect him from office gossip and malicious jokes about his drinking (pp. 145–146).
adfbb1780c3b: He may overwork; encourage him to play, and allow reasonable time for helping other alcoholics, which is "necessary to maintain his sobriety" (p. 146).
f9ee11fad9a2: "Your man may be trusted." (p. 146). If he does drink and is really trying, he'll tell you, even at the cost of his job.
7184fc04dcf6: If he stumbles, you decide whether to keep him; "you should feel under no obligation to keep him on, for your obligation has been well discharged already" (p. 147).
19939af7b88f: Give junior executives the book, so they stop covering for drinking employees and can be fair and square with them (pp. 147–148).
c5e8b103e185: Many firms think they have no alcoholic problem; it might pay "to take another look down the line" (p. 149). The chapter is about alcoholics, "sick people," not the habitual or whoopee drinker, for whom a strict policy is "undoubtedly sound" (p. 149).
c5bec41944b8: The writer ends with his own small company, where two alcoholic employees "produce as much as five normal salesmen" (p. 150).
8c0a3c607526: The chapter speaks to employers as employers. It doesn't ask them to join or support A.A. It hopes employees may be "put in personal contact with some of us" (p. 144), and says a great deal can be done with the book alone. Appendix VI gives A.A.'s address for anyone who wants help (p. 150, note).

6cc519874f0a: What happened to Bill W. at Towns Hospital?
ed938069c469: Towns Hospital in New York, where Dr. William D. Silkworth was the physician, treated Bill W. several times. On his last stay, in December 1934, a few weeks after his friend Ebby's visit, Bill had the sudden spiritual experience that ended his drinking.
4c471c591acb: The 1939 Big Book tells it quietly: in the hospital he offered himself to God, became willing to have his sins taken away, and felt a peace and a "great clean wind of a mountain top" blow through him. He asked the doctor if he was still sane; the doctor said something had happened he didn't understand, but Bill had better hang on to it.
48e05d00cdec: Bill's later accounts add a cry of despair ("If there is a God, let Him show Himself!"), a room lit with white light, and a sense of Presence. They also give the doctor's reassurance in different words.
8967faddf4b0: Silkworth's own letter in the Big Book says the idea that led to A.A. came to this patient "in the course of his third treatment."
93be108d338a: <0>"Bill's Story."</0> On an earlier stay at "a nationally-known hospital for the mental and physical rehabilitation of alcoholics" (p. 7), "Under the so-called belladonna treatment my brain cleared." (p. 7), and a kind doctor explained that he had been seriously ill, bodily and mentally (p. 7). He drank again, went back, and his wife was told he would die or go mad within a year (p. 7).
8d1326b690e7: After Ebby's visit, he went back once more. "At the hospital I was separated from alcohol for the last time." (p. 13). "There I humbly offered myself to God, as I then understood Him, to do with me as He would." (p. 13). His friend visited, and they made a list of the people Bill had hurt (p. 13). When Bill fully accepted these proposals, "the effect was electric. There was a sense of victory, followed by such a peace and serenity as I had never known." (p. 14). "I felt lifted up, as though the great clean wind of a mountain top blew through and through." (p. 14). "God comes to most men gradually, but His impact on me was sudden and profound." (p. 14).
641739287a4b: Alarmed, he asked the doctor if he was still sane. The doctor said: "Something has happened to you I don't understand. But you had better hang on to it." (p. 14). Still in the hospital, Bill thought of the thousands of hopeless alcoholics he might help (p. 14). The 1939 text names neither the hospital nor the doctor; the names come from later accounts.
ca44a1eb9dd0: <0>"The Doctor's Opinion."</0> Dr. Silkworth's letter, also from 1939, doesn't name Bill: "In late 1934 I attended a patient who, though he had been a competent businessman of good earning capacity, was an alcoholic of a type I had come to regard as hopeless." (p. xxv). "In the course of his third treatment he acquired certain ideas concerning a possible means of recovery." (p. xxv). See <1>What is "The Doctor's Opinion," and who wrote it?</1>
80c5d435a3e3: Bill's later accounts (1957, and as told in 1984)
5a26223e433f: <0>A.A. Comes of Age (1957).</0> In the summer of 1934 Bill lay in Towns, and Dr. Silkworth told Lois he was hopeless (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). In December, after Ebby's visit and a night at the Calvary Mission, he walked into Towns carrying a bottle of beer (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "In three or four days I was free of what little sedative they gave me" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957), but very depressed and still choking on the idea of God. Ebby came and repeated his formula (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Then, at the bottom of the pit, he cried out: "If there is a God, let Him show Himself! I am ready to do anything, anything!" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). The room lit up with a great white light; he felt he was on a mountain in a wind of spirit, and that he was a free man (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). "So this is the God of the preachers!" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
d8caf7a8c2db: Frightened that he was hallucinating, he called the doctor, who said: "No, Bill, you are not crazy." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Elsewhere in the same book Bill quotes him: "you are not hallucinating" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). 8d1e3efbb6d7: The one firm line is at the level of the public media: no full names or pictures as A.A. members in the press, radio or film. Everything closer to home is left to each member and group.

7eca47299640: <0>What anonymity means.</0> The word "anonymous" reminds members to put principles before personalities, and shows that the movement has given up personal glorification in public (P-17, p. 41).

"We have dropped anonymity at this level because we think our friends and associates ought to know about Alcoholics Anonymous" (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946, p. 44), and because members wanted to lose the fear of admitting they were alcoholics. Members often spoke under their own names at semipublic gatherings, asking only that reporters not print them (P-17, p. 44).
99b5d6935439: <0>Where the line is.</0> If every member felt free to publish his own name, picture and story, A.A. would be launched on endless personal publicity, so the line has to be drawn there (P-17, p. 44). Bill proposed three points (P-17, p. 44): 1. It is "the privilege of each A.A. to cloak himself" in as much anonymity as he wants, and others should respect that (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946, p. 44). 2. A member should respect his own group's feeling about anonymity in their town. 3. No member should publish his name or picture in public media in connection with A.A. activity, though he can use his name in other public activities so long as he doesn't disclose his A.A. membership.
8f62f094dcfd: <0>Protecting newcomers.</0> A newcomer's anonymity should be kept as long as he wants it, even under an assumed name, because A.A. promised it when he came (P-17, p. 46).
93e47e7388c6: <0>Secrecy is a mistake too.</0> Groups that shut themselves away year after year grow stale and forget "their obligation to other alcoholics in their communities" (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946, p. 46). See <1>Tradition Eleven: does A.A. advertise?</1>
c139109f0588: <0>His summary.</0> With one important exception, how far each member or group drops anonymity is "left strictly to the individual or group concerned" (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946, p. 47). The exception is publication: writing or speaking for publication as A.A. members, nobody discloses their full name (P-17, p. 47).
eaf31dd00019: Nine years later he was just as clear: "no A.A. need be anonymous to" family, friends or neighbors, and telling them is usually right and good (P-17, "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous", 1955, p. 56). Speaking at group or semipublic A.A. meetings carries no special danger, "provided, press reports reveal first names only" (P-17, "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous", 1955, p. 56). It's humility (no personal glory from A.A.) plus one public rule (no names and faces as A.A. members in the media), plus respect for anyone who wants to stay private.
